items.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995
items.q: And a friend of mine and I, we went to school together, named Johnny Bratton.

ctx.x: Well first of all it’s a great pleasure to be here. We’ve had some interesting conversations with some other fine musicians, and Red Holloway has been on our list, and we’re glad to have him here as an alto and tenor saxophonist. And we wondered, one thing we are interested in is how jazz has changed over the years for you — what made you want to get into music as a kid, and just some things about your own career that you could share with us.

Well, see I’ll be 68 years old this year. And when I was a kid, you could either be a Pullman porter, you could become a barber, if your folks had money you might be able to become a doctor. But if you had no talents and you were nice looking, you could become a pimp. But basically most people became, most men became Pullman porters. So I had none of those qualifications, and since my mother was a pianist and my father played violin, I decided maybe I should try to be a musician. But I always liked boxing…

like, well you made $2.50 an hour as a musician. And when you were making $6.00 a night and all you could eat and drink, that was good money. So basically that’s when I decided I really wanted to be a musician. And even though the money wasn’t an awful lot, you know, there wasn’t a requirement, the cost of living was down, so you didn’t have to pay a lot of money. You could rent a house for like $20 a month, stuff like that. And it was very cheap. Of course you didn’t make a lot of money but it didn’t cost a lot…
